2027-06-29.title: Saints Peter and Paul, Apostles

2027-06-29.alt: Solemnity. Mass during the Day. Gloria and Creed. The Vigil Mass, with its own readings (Acts 3:1–10; Psalm 19; Galatians 1:11–20; John 21:15–19), was celebrated yesterday evening. In Rome the Holy Father blesses the pallia for the metropolitan archbishops appointed during the past year. A day to pray especially for Pope Leo XIV. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-06-29.verse: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
theo: Today the Church honours together the two apostles on whom, under Christ, she was built: Peter the fisherman of Galilee, to whom Jesus gave the keys, and Paul the scholar of Tarsus, who carried the Gospel to the nations. They were very different men, and they once disagreed openly at Antioch (Galatians 2:11). But they confessed the same Lord, served the same Church, and according to the ancient tradition of the Church of Rome both gave their lives for Christ in that city under the emperor Nero, in the mid-60s of the first century: Peter crucified, tradition says head downwards, near the Vatican Hill, and Paul beheaded outside the walls on the road to Ostia. Their tombs have been venerated there ever since, and over them stand St Peter's Basilica and the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls. That is why they share one feast. The first reading shows Peter in chains. King Herod Agrippa I, wanting to win favour, has already “had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword,” the first of the Twelve to die for Christ, and now he arrests Peter during the Passover festival, guarded by “four squads of soldiers.” The future looks clear: Peter will be next. But Luke tells us what the Church was doing: “While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.” And on the very night before his trial, Peter is “sleeping between two soldiers,” bound with two chains. He sleeps, because he has put his life in the Lord's hands. Then the cell fills with light; an angel taps him: “Get up quickly.” The chains fall off, the iron gate opens “of its own accord,” and Peter, who thought he was dreaming, finds himself in the street and says: “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me.” Peter's deliverance is also a picture of Easter: the night, the command to rise, the gate that opens. The Psalm is Peter's song: “I sought the LORD, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears,” and “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.”

The second reading is Paul's farewell. Writing from prison in Rome to his beloved Timothy, he knows that the end has come: “As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation, and the time of my departure has come.” A libation was wine poured out on the altar over a sacrifice; Paul sees his coming death as an offering poured out for Christ. Then he looks back over his life with three images, from the army, the stadium and the treasury: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” He does not boast; he gives thanks, and he waits for “the crown of righteousness” that the Lord will give “not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing.” He knows what it is to be abandoned by friends, but adds: “the Lord stood by me and gave me strength, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it.” Peter was rescued from prison; Paul says, “I was rescued from the lion's mouth,” and is sure that the Lord will rescue him “from every evil attack and save me for his heavenly kingdom.” For both apostles the final rescue was not escape from death but passage through death into the kingdom. Paul's last word is not about himself: “To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”

The Gospel takes us north to Caesarea Philippi, a city built by Herod's son Philip near a great rock cliff with a shrine to the pagan god Pan. There, far from Jerusalem, among the gods of the nations, Jesus asks two questions. The first is easy: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” The disciples report the opinions: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet. The second cannot be answered by reporting what others say: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon speaks for all: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.” Jesus calls him blessed, and tells him that this confession is not human cleverness: “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.” Then Jesus gives him a new name and a mission. In Aramaic the word play is exact: “you are Kepha, and on this kepha I will build my church”: you are Rock, and on this rock. A rock is what does not move when the storm comes. Jesus promises that “the gates of Hades,” the power of death, “will not prevail against” his Church. And he gives Peter “the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Every Jew knew the words of Isaiah about the chief steward of the king's house: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open, and no one shall shut” (Isaiah 22:22). The steward governs the household in the king's name. To “bind” and “loose” means to forbid and permit, to exclude and to reconcile, with authority that heaven confirms. The Catholic Church believes that this ministry of Peter did not end with Peter, because the Church still needs a rock and a steward until the Lord returns. The Bishop of Rome, the successor of Peter, is “the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful” (Lumen Gentium 23; Catechism 882). And Peter's weakness did not cancel his mission: the same man would deny Jesus three times, and be asked three times by the risen Lord, “Do you love me?” and told, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17). The Church is founded not on Peter's strength, but on Christ's prayer for him: “I have prayed for you that your own faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Today we thank God for Peter and Paul, for the faith we received through them, and for Pope Leo XIV, who sits today in Peter's chair.
conn: Caesarea Philippi.

A city at the foot of Mount Hermon, at the sources of the Jordan, rebuilt by Herod's son Philip and named after Caesar. A rock cliff there held a shrine to the god Pan. Jesus asks his question among the gods of the nations.
“Son of the living God.”
Peter's confession goes beyond calling Jesus the Messiah: he is the Son of the living God. The Catechism sees here the faith on which the Church is built (Catechism 424, 442).
Peter, Kepha.
Jesus gives Simon the name Kepha, Aramaic for “rock,” translated into Greek as Petros (John 1:42). Paul usually calls him Cephas (Galatians 1:18).
“My church.”
The Greek ekklesia translates the Hebrew qahal, the assembly of God's people at Sinai. Jesus speaks of “my” Church: he builds it, and it belongs to him.
“The gates of Hades.”
Hades is the realm of the dead; its “gates” are the power of death. Christ promises that death will not overcome his Church.
The keys.
Isaiah 22:22: the master of the palace receives the key of the house of David. Keys mean authority to govern the house in the king's name (Catechism 553).
“Bind and loose.”

Rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting, and for excluding from and readmitting to the community. Peter receives this authority personally; the apostles share it with him (Matthew 18:18; Catechism 553, 1444).
Herod Agrippa I.
Grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea from AD 41 to 44. He executed James, son of Zebedee, around AD 44 (Acts 12:2).
“Poured out as a libation.”
A drink offering poured over a sacrifice (Numbers 28:7). Paul uses the same image in Philippians 2:17.
The pallium.

A narrow band of white wool marked with black crosses, worn over the shoulders by the Pope and by metropolitan archbishops as a sign of their communion with the successor of Peter and of the shepherd who carries the sheep. The pallia are blessed by the Pope on this solemnity.
altar: At every Mass we pray by name for our Pope and our bishop. This is not a formality: the Eucharist is the sacrament of the Church's unity, and the communion of each altar with the bishop, and of every bishop with the successor of Peter, is the sign that we share the one faith of the apostles. Peter and Paul are named in the Roman Canon among the apostles whose merits and prayers we ask.

Paul spoke of his life as poured out like a libation over the sacrifice. At the altar the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, and our lives, like those of the apostles, are poured out with his. Peter, who was told to feed the Lord's sheep, fed them with the Word and with the Bread of Life; that same food is given to us today.
outline: Ask: if Jesus turned to you today and asked, “But who do you say that I am?”, what would you answer, not from a book but from your heart?
Point 1 · Who do you say that I am?
Peter's confession, revealed by the Father, is the faith of the Church.
Point 2 · On this rock, the keys
Christ builds his Church on Peter and gives him the keys: the ministry of the successor of Peter today.
Peter in chains, the praying Church, and the angel who opens the gate.
Point 4 · I have kept the faith
Paul's farewell: a life poured out, a race finished, a crown waiting.
Two tombs in Rome, a fisherman's and a tentmaker's, with great basilicas built over them, and pilgrims from every nation praying the same Creed.
“You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
live: Pray today, and every day this week, for Pope Leo XIV: an Our Father, a Hail Mary and a Glory Be, or the prayer: Lord, guard him, give him life, make him blessed on earth.
Write down in one sentence your own answer to Jesus' question: Who do you say that I am? Keep it in your Bible.
Name one area where you are tempted to give up, in prayer, in marriage, in work, in the fight against a sin, and ask St Paul's help to finish the race.
Learn the faith of the apostles
Read slowly this week the Apostles' Creed, one article each day, and ask what each article means for your life.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon on the feast, in substance)

One day is kept for the passion of two apostles, but these two were one. Though they suffered on different days, they were one. Peter went first, Paul followed. Let us keep this feast, made holy for us by the blood of the apostles; let us love their faith, their life, their labours, their sufferings.
St Leo the Great (Sermon 82, in substance)
These are the men through whom the light of Christ's Gospel shone on you, O Rome. They are your holy fathers and true shepherds, who founded you far better than those who built your walls.
Where Peter is, there is the Church; where the Church is, there death is not, but life eternal.
magis: Peter's confession and the keys of the kingdom: the authority to govern the house of God, to bind and to loose.
The Lord made Simon alone the rock of his Church; the Roman Pontiff, as successor of Peter, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of unity.
Vatican II: Christ set Peter over the other apostles; the college of bishops has authority only together with its head, the Roman Pontiff.
The Lord gave his Church a structure that will remain until the Kingdom is fully achieved: the Twelve with Peter as their head.
In giving Peter the power to bind and loose, Christ gave the apostles' ministry the authority to reconcile sinners with the Church.
saints: Sts Peter and Paul in history

Simon Peter, a fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum, head of the Twelve, preached in Jerusalem, Antioch and Rome; his two letters are in the New Testament. Paul, a Pharisee of Tarsus, converted on the road to Damascus, made at least three great missionary journeys and wrote letters that form much of the New Testament. Both were martyred in Rome under Nero (c. 64–67). The Church of Rome has kept their feast together on 29 June since ancient times; it already appears in a Roman calendar of the year 354.
30 Jun: the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church (optional memorial), the Christians killed in Nero's persecution. 3 Jul: St Thomas the Apostle, the Apostle of India.
2027-06-29.prayer: O God, who on the Solemnity of the Apostles Peter and Paul give us the noble and holy joys of this day, grant, we pray, that your Church may in all things follow the teaching of those through whom she received the beginnings of right religion. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you asked your disciples: Who do you say that I am? With Peter we answer: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Keep your Church built on the rock, and let the gates of Hades never prevail against her. Strengthen Pope Leo XIV, the successor of Peter, and all the bishops in communion with him. Give us Paul's courage to fight the good fight, finish the race and keep the faith, and bring us at last, with your apostles, to your heavenly kingdom. Amen.

quick: King Herod kills James and imprisons Peter; while the Church prays fervently, an angel leads Peter out of prison.
Paul, near death in Rome, says: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; the Lord stood by me.
Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God; Jesus calls him the rock on which he will build his Church and gives him the keys of the kingdom.
2027-06-29.action: Pray today for Pope Leo XIV and for your bishop by name.
2027-06-29.question: Who is Jesus for me: an opinion I have heard, or the Son of the living God whom I confess?

Why is the Pope the visible foundation of the Church's unity?
Why is the Church called apostolic?
kidsaint: Peter was a fisherman with rough hands and a big heart. He sometimes spoke too fast and once even said he did not know Jesus. But Jesus forgave him and made him the leader of the apostles, the rock of the Church. Paul at first hated Christians, but Jesus met him on the road to Damascus, and he became the greatest missionary, travelling by land and sea to tell everyone about Jesus. Both of them died for Jesus in Rome. Lesson: Jesus can use anyone who loves him, even people who have made big mistakes.
2027-06-29.special: Solemnity of Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles. Gloria and Creed. Mass during the Day (the Vigil Mass was celebrated yesterday evening). The Pope blesses the pallia for new metropolitan archbishops. Pray for Pope Leo XIV.
term: A narrow circular band of white lamb's wool with six black crosses, worn over the chasuble around the shoulders. The Pope wears it, and so do metropolitan archbishops, as a sign of their authority as shepherds and of their communion with the successor of Peter. The wool recalls the lost sheep that the Good Shepherd carries on his shoulders. New archbishops receive the pallium blessed by the Pope on the solemnity of Sts Peter and Paul.

family.explain: Jesus asked his friends: who do people say that I am? Then he asked: but who do you say that I am? Peter answered: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God! Jesus said: you are Peter, which means rock, and on this rock I will build my Church. Today the Pope, who lives in Rome, is the one who takes Peter's place, to keep the Church together. That is why we pray for him every day.
family.intention: We pray for Pope Leo XIV, for our bishop and our priests, and for Christians who are in prison or persecuted for their faith.
family.ask: Ask: “Can each of us say in our own words who Jesus is for us?” Then pray together one Our Father for the Pope.

illus: During the monsoon fishing ban, when the big boats stay ashore, an old fisherman in a coastal parish near Thiruvananthapuram spends his mornings mending nets in the shade beside the church of St Peter. His name, like many on that coast, is Pathrose. A seminarian home for the holidays once asked him why he always ended his rosary with a prayer for the Pope. He said: my patron was a fisherman who sometimes sank in the water and sometimes ran away. Jesus still made him the rock. If Jesus could hold Peter up, he can hold up the Pope, and he can hold me up too. But the Pope has the heaviest net in the world to mend, so I help him with my beads. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you built your Church on the rock of Peter and sent Paul to the nations. Make us firm in the faith of the apostles. Amen.
share: But who do you say that I am? (Matthew 16:15). How would I answer Jesus today, in my own words?
While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him (Acts 12:5). For which imprisoned or suffering person or Church is God asking me to pray fervently?
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). Where do I need courage not to give up?
pm.resp: The angel of the Lord will rescue those who fear him.
interc: For Pope Leo XIV, successor of Peter, that the Lord may strengthen him to confirm his brothers in faith and to keep the Church in unity.
For the new metropolitan archbishops who receive the pallium, and for our own bishop.
For Christians imprisoned or persecuted for their faith, that the Church may pray for them as she prayed for Peter.
For missionaries, especially in India and Asia, that like Paul they may proclaim the word fully so that all nations may hear it.
For unity among all Christians, that the Churches may one day share the one table of the Lord.
pm.close: Father, you gave us the apostles Peter and Paul as our fathers in faith. Keep us in their teaching and bring us to share their crown. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church celebrates two great men together, Peter and Paul. They were very different. Peter was a fisherman from Galilee, with rough hands and a quick tongue. Paul was a learned man from Tarsus, a Pharisee who once persecuted the Church. They even argued with each other. But Christ made them the two pillars of his Church, and both gave their lives for him in Rome. Over their tombs stand today two great basilicas, and from every nation pilgrims come to pray there.

In the Gospel Jesus asks his disciples: who do people say that the Son of Man is? That is an easy question. We can all report what others say about Jesus: a good teacher, a prophet, a great man. Then comes the hard question: but who do you say that I am? (Matthew 16:15). Nobody can answer that for us, not our parents, not the priest. Peter answers: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. And Jesus says: flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven. Faith is a gift. Let us ask for it today.

Then Jesus says to Peter: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:18–19). A rock that holds firm, keys that open and close. Jesus knew that his Church would need a visible shepherd to keep it together. That ministry did not end with Peter. Today it is carried by Pope Leo XIV. We do not follow the Pope because he is clever or because we like him; we follow him because Christ built his Church on Peter and his successors. And we pray for him, because his burden is heavy.

Do not forget: this rock was a weak man. Peter sank in the water. He denied Jesus three times. But the Lord prayed for him that his faith might not fail, and after the Resurrection asked him three times: do you love me? Feed my sheep. The Church is not built on Peter's strength but on Christ's mercy to Peter. That gives hope to all of us who are weak.

In the first reading Peter is in prison, chained between two soldiers, waiting for death. And what does the Church do? While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him (Acts 12:5). And the chains fell off. Dear friends, there are Christians in prison today, in many countries, also in our own. There are priests and bishops under pressure. Do we pray for them fervently? Peter was rescued by the prayer of the Church.

And Paul, at the end of his life, writes from prison: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). Could we say that at the end of our lives? Let us ask Peter to give us his faith, and Paul to give us his courage. And let us leave this church today with Peter's answer in our hearts and on our lips: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Amen.
kids: Children, today we celebrate two of Jesus' best friends, Peter and Paul. Peter was a fisherman. Jesus asked him: who do you say that I am? Peter said: you are the Son of God! Jesus said: you are Peter, the rock! I will build my Church on you, and I will give you the keys of heaven. Today the Pope takes Peter's place, and we pray for him.

Paul travelled far, far away, on ships and on foot, to tell people about Jesus. At the end of his life he said: I ran the race and I kept the faith! Let us ask Peter and Paul to help us love Jesus and tell others about him. And tonight, say one Hail Mary for the Pope.

intro: Theme: “But who do you say that I am?”
The faith of Peter, the keys of the kingdom, the praying Church, and Paul's race finished: two pillars of one Church.
